A.5.1: Keep security policy aligned with management direction and make it usable by the people expected to follow it.
Approved policies, ownership, communication and review records.
A.5.2: Assign security responsibilities so important decisions and activities have accountable owners.
Responsibility matrix, role descriptions and communicated assignments.
A.5.3: Separate duties that could allow one person to misuse a process without an appropriate check.
Role design, access assignments, approval paths and compensating review records.
A.5.4: Management should make security expectations clear and support their application in day-to-day work.
Management communications, team responsibilities and follow-up records.
A.5.5: Maintain appropriate relationships and contact routes with relevant authorities.
Authority contact list, assigned liaison responsibilities and relevant correspondence.
A.5.6: Use relevant security communities and professional contacts to stay informed and obtain appropriate support.
Participation records, information received and examples of resulting action.
A.5.7: Use relevant threat information to inform security decisions rather than collecting intelligence without a purpose.
Threat sources, analysis notes and linked risk or operational decisions.
A.5.8: Include security needs in projects while decisions can still influence design and delivery.
Project security requirements, review gates and accepted exceptions.
A.5.9: Know what information and related assets exist and who is responsible for managing them.
Asset/data inventories, assigned owners and reconciliation records.
A.5.10: Define acceptable ways to use information and assets so users understand the boundaries.
A.5.11: Recover organizational assets when a person or relationship no longer needs them.
Asset assignment lists, departure checklists and return records.
A.5.12: Classify information according to its protection needs and business context.
Classification scheme, data inventory and owner decisions.
A.5.13: Make information classifications recognizable where labels help people or systems handle data appropriately.
Labelling guidance, labelled samples and applicable tool settings.
A.5.14: Protect information when it is transferred between people, systems or organizations.
Transfer procedures, agreement terms and relevant channel configurations.
A.5.15: Establish access rules that connect business need to appropriate information and system permissions.
Access policy, role definitions and approval criteria.
A.5.16: Manage identities through creation, change and retirement rather than only at initial provisioning.
Identity records, provisioning/change tickets and deactivation evidence.
A.5.17: Handle authentication information so credentials are issued, protected and changed appropriately.
Credential-handling procedures and configuration evidence without credential values.
A.5.18: Approve, review, change and remove access rights as people's responsibilities and needs change.
Access approvals, review records and revocation tickets.
A.5.19: Manage the security exposure introduced by supplier relationships.
Supplier inventory, risk assessments and accountable business owners.
A.5.20: Include appropriate security expectations in supplier agreements.
Security clauses, negotiated requirements and approved agreement records.
A.5.21: Consider security risks across the technology supply chain, not just the direct supplier.
Technology supplier assessments, dependency records and supply-chain risk decisions.
A.5.22: Review supplier service performance and manage changes that affect security.
Service reviews, assurance follow-up and change records.
A.5.23: Manage cloud use deliberately through acquisition, operation and exit, including shared responsibilities.
Cloud inventory, responsibility model, configuration reviews and exit arrangements.
A.5.24: Prepare the roles, procedures and resources needed to handle security incidents.
Incident plan, responsibilities, contact routes and exercise records.
A.5.25: Assess security events and decide which require incident response.
Triage criteria, event records and escalation decisions.
A.5.26: Carry out a coordinated response when a security incident is identified.
Response procedures, incident timelines and recorded actions.
A.5.27: Use incident experience to improve the security program.
Lessons-learned records, assigned improvements and follow-up validation.
A.5.28: Preserve incident-related evidence in a way that supports its intended use and traceability.
Evidence-handling procedure, collection records and provenance.
A.5.29: Maintain appropriate information security while operating under disruptive conditions.
Continuity procedures, emergency access decisions and exercise results.
A.5.30: Prepare technology to support the organization's continuity needs.
Recovery requirements, plans, dependency information and test results.
A.5.31: Identify and manage the obligations relevant to information security within the ISMS scope.
Obligations register, assigned owners and review records.
A.5.32: Protect intellectual property and manage the rights associated with material the organization uses.
Licensing records, usage rules and intellectual-property handling procedures.
A.5.33: Protect business records against inappropriate loss, change, disclosure or destruction.
Record-retention rules, access settings and preservation/disposal records.
A.5.34: Address personal-information protection in the organization's actual processing activities.
Data-flow records, privacy responsibilities and relevant handling safeguards.
A.5.35: Obtain an appropriately independent evaluation of the security approach and its implementation.
Review scope, reviewer independence, results and corrective follow-up.
A.5.36: Check whether security practices follow the organization's established rules.
Compliance reviews, exceptions and corrective-action records.
A.5.37: Make operating instructions available where consistent and safe execution depends on them.
Current procedures, controlled access and execution records.
A.6.1: Use appropriate checks before employment in light of the role and applicable constraints.
Screening procedure and completion records with sensitive details minimized.
A.6.2: Make employment-related security responsibilities clear in the relevant terms and commitments.
Employment terms, role expectations and acknowledgement records.
A.6.3: Provide security learning suited to people's responsibilities and the environment they work in.
Training content, audience assignments, completion and follow-up records.
A.6.4: Handle security-policy violations through an established and communicated disciplinary process.
Disciplinary procedure and appropriately restricted case records.
A.6.5: Manage security duties that change or continue when employment or roles change.
Departure/transfer checklists, access changes and continuing obligations.
A.6.6: Establish appropriate confidentiality commitments for people who access protected information.
Confidentiality agreements, scope and review records.
A.6.7: Protect information and assets used away from the organization's normal workplace.
Remote-work rules, endpoint/access configurations and exception decisions.
A.6.8: Give people a clear way to report suspected security events promptly.
Reporting instructions, workforce communications and received reports.
A.7.1: Define physical boundaries that protect areas containing sensitive information and assets.
Site layout, perimeter protections and boundary review records.
A.7.2: Control who enters protected locations and under what conditions.
Entry procedures, access lists and visitor records.
A.7.3: Apply physical protection appropriate to the offices, rooms and facilities in scope.
Facility safeguards, access restrictions and inspection records.
A.7.4: Detect and respond to unauthorized physical access or intrusion.
Physical monitoring configuration, alert handling and review records.
A.7.5: Address environmental and physical hazards that could affect information or technology.
Site risk assessments, protection measures and inspection/test records.
A.7.6: Define safe working practices for people operating in protected areas.
Secure-area procedures, access responsibilities and applicable work records.
A.7.7: Reduce exposure from unattended documents, media and screens.
Clear-desk/screen rules, lock settings and workplace review observations.
A.7.8: Place and protect equipment to reduce relevant physical and environmental risks.
Equipment layout, protective measures and site review records.
A.7.9: Protect organizational assets when used or stored off-site.
Off-site asset records, handling rules and loss/exception follow-up.
A.7.10: Protect storage media throughout its use, movement, reuse and disposal.
Media handling procedures, transfer records and disposal evidence.
A.7.11: Address dependence on power and other utilities needed for reliable operation.
Utility resilience arrangements, maintenance and test results.
A.7.12: Protect cabling against relevant damage, interference or unauthorized access.
Cabling layout, protective measures and inspection records.
A.7.13: Maintain equipment without exposing information or undermining security.
Maintenance arrangements, service records and access controls.
A.7.14: Remove information and protect assets appropriately before equipment is reused or retired.
Retirement procedures, sanitization verification and disposal records.
A.8.1: Protect user endpoints according to the information and activities they support.
Endpoint baseline, coverage reports and exception records.
A.8.2: Restrict and oversee elevated privileges that can bypass ordinary protections.
Privileged access approvals, account inventory and review records.
A.8.3: Limit information access according to the established authorization rules.
Role/permission configuration, access decisions and review results.
A.8.4: Control access to source code and related development assets.
Repository access settings, approval records and access reviews.
A.8.5: Use authentication appropriate to the sensitivity and risks of the access path.
Authentication configurations, enforcement coverage and exceptions.
A.8.6: Monitor and plan resource capacity to support the required service levels.
Capacity measures, forecasts and corrective capacity decisions.
A.8.7: Prevent, detect and address malicious software within the assessed scope.
Malware protection settings, deployment coverage and detection follow-up.
A.8.8: Identify technical weaknesses and manage their treatment according to risk.
Vulnerability reports, prioritized remediation and verified closure records.
A.8.9: Establish and maintain approved configurations rather than leaving system settings unmanaged.
Configuration baselines, compliance checks and change/exception records.
A.8.10: Remove information when it is no longer needed under the applicable retention and handling decisions.
Deletion procedures, retention configuration and execution records.
A.8.11: Reduce unnecessary exposure of sensitive values when full data is not needed.
Masking rules, scoped configuration and representative output samples.
A.8.12: Detect or prevent inappropriate movement or disclosure of information.
Data-loss prevention rules, coverage and alert follow-up.
A.8.13: Maintain backups that support the organization's recovery needs and verify their usability.
Backup scope, protected-copy configuration, job results and restore tests.
A.8.14: Provide redundancy where it supports the availability needs of information processing.
Resilience design, failover configuration and test results.
A.8.15: Generate and protect event records that support accountability and investigation.
Logging scope, event samples, retention and access settings.
A.8.16: Monitor relevant activity and investigate signs of adverse behavior.
Monitoring coverage, detection rules and investigation records.
A.8.17: Keep system clocks aligned so records from different systems can be interpreted together.
Time-source configuration and synchronization health records.
A.8.18: Control tools that can override normal system or application safeguards.
Privileged-tool inventory, access approvals and usage logs.
A.8.19: Control software installation on operational systems.
Installation rules, administrative permissions and approved deployment records.
A.8.20: Protect networks and connected information against the relevant security threats.
Network design, protection configurations and reviewed exceptions.
A.8.21: Define and manage the safeguards expected from network services.
Network-service requirements, agreements and configuration/monitoring records.
A.8.22: Separate network areas where doing so limits inappropriate access or the spread of an incident.
Segmentation design, traffic rules and verification results.
A.8.23: Manage access to external web content according to the organization's security needs.
Web-filtering policy, configured coverage and exception records.
A.8.24: Use cryptography and manage keys in a way that supports the identified protection needs.
Cryptographic policy, key-management responsibilities and configuration records without keys.
A.8.25: Build security into the software-development lifecycle rather than adding it only at release.
Development process, security gates and delivery records.
A.8.26: Identify application security needs while defining or acquiring the application.
Security requirements, acceptance criteria and risk decisions.
A.8.27: Apply security principles to system design and architecture.
Architecture principles, design reviews and documented trade-offs.
A.8.28: Use coding practices that reduce security defects in software.
Coding standards, review evidence and relevant analysis results.
A.8.29: Test security before accepting software or systems into their intended use.
Test scope, results, defect remediation and acceptance decisions.
A.8.30: Oversee security in development performed by external parties.
Supplier development requirements, review records and deliverable acceptance.
A.8.31: Separate development, testing and production so changes or testing do not inappropriately affect live operations.
Environment boundaries, access permissions and deployment paths.
A.8.32: Assess and control changes that affect information processing.
Change requests, impact assessments, approvals and implementation checks.
A.8.33: Protect the information used for testing, especially when it resembles or originates from sensitive live data.
Test-data handling rules, access restrictions and masking/deletion records.
A.8.34: Plan audit testing so it does not unnecessarily disrupt or expose operational systems.
Agreed test scope, safeguards, authorization and test records.

groups.4: Typical implementation connects the organization's context, obligations and scope to the actual ISMS processes. Check whether important interfaces or dependencies fall outside a narrowly written scope.
groups.5: Typical implementation ties leadership direction to approved policy, accountable roles and decisions that demonstrate management involvement.
groups.6: Typical implementation links planning decisions to risk criteria, accountable owners, treatment and measurable objectives. Check follow-through and planned changes, not just the existence of a plan.
groups.7: Typical implementation makes resources, competence, communications and controlled documentation available to the people operating the ISMS.
groups.8: Typical implementation demonstrates that planned processes and risk treatments are carried out and that significant changes trigger appropriate reassessment.
groups.9: Typical implementation connects performance evidence, independent internal audit and management review to recorded conclusions and follow-up decisions. Preserve the distinction between an audit and a management review.
groups.10: Typical implementation links identified weaknesses to causes, corrective work and a check of effectiveness. Completing an Action alone does not establish that the underlying issue is resolved.
groups.A.5: Depending on the control, typical implementation connects documented responsibilities and procedures to actual decisions and operating records. Explain the risk-based SoA selection and check that practice covers the relevant information, services and relationships.
groups.A.6: Typical implementation covers the relevant workforce and relationship stages, assigns responsibility and preserves appropriate evidence of execution while protecting personnel information.
groups.A.7: Typical implementation reflects actual facilities, equipment and media, including remote locations and exceptions. Check physical arrangements and operating records rather than relying only on a facilities policy.
groups.A.8: Typical implementation maps the technical measure to in-scope systems, verifies deployment and documents exceptions. Check actual operation and coverage rather than treating a purchased tool or written standard as sufficient.
